result: The NY-ESO-1 S-FLU virus system is a pseudotyped replication-deficient influenza virus that can express exogenous proteins. In vitro infection demonstrates expression of both influenza NP (nuclear localization) and NY-ESO-1 (cytoplasmic localization) proteins in infected cells, with the HA component being exchangeable across virus subtypes.
evaluation: Claims C1, C2, C8-C10 are well-supported by the cited prior work (Powell et al., 2012) and immunofluorescence data (Figure 1—figure supplement 1) showing proper protein expression and subcellular localization. The system design and functionality are clearly demonstrated.

result: Intranasal infection with NY-ESO-1 S-FLU virus in BALB/c mice results in preferential infection of EpCAM+ lung epithelial cells compared to CD45+ immune cells on day 2 post-infection.
evaluation: Claims C11-C12 are supported by flow cytometry data in Figure 1—figure supplement 2 showing differential infection rates between epithelial and immune cell populations. The data clearly demonstrate tissue tropism of the virus.

result: NY-ESO-1 S-FLU virus infection induces antigen-specific T cell priming in draining lymph nodes, as demonstrated by proliferation of adoptively transferred 1G4 T cells.
evaluation: Claims C13-C14 are supported by CellTrace Violet proliferation data (Figure 1—figure supplement 3) showing specific proliferation only in NY-ESO-1 S-FLU infected mice. This demonstrates functional antigen presentation and T cell priming.

result: Intranasal infection with NY-ESO-1 S-FLU virus elicits robust NY-ESO-1-specific CTL responses in lungs and spleen of HHD and BALB/c mice, though at lower magnitude than responses to immunodominant influenza epitopes. The virus demonstrates specific cytotoxic activity in vivo.
evaluation: Claims C15-C18 are well-supported by flow cytometry data (Figure 1B, Figure 1—figure supplement 4) and in vivo killing assays (Figure 1C). The comparative analysis with influenza epitopes provides appropriate context for the magnitude of response.

result: NY-ESO-1 S-FLU virus provides significant protection against tumor challenge in prophylactic, therapeutic, and spontaneous metastasis models. A single infection is sufficient for prophylactic protection, while two sequential infections are required for therapeutic efficacy and optimal reduction of spontaneous metastasis.
evaluation: Claims C19-C24 are supported by tumor nodule enumeration and clonogenic assay data (Figure 2A-C) with appropriate statistical analysis (p<0.05). The dose-response relationship and model-dependent efficacy are clearly demonstrated.

result: Intranasal infection induces strong lung CTL responses but weak systemic responses, failing to protect against subcutaneous tumors. This motivates investigation of intramuscular delivery based on prior literature showing systemic CTL generation.
evaluation: Claims C25-C28 are supported by experimental data (Figures 1—figure supplement 4, 3A) and appropriate citations (Spitzer et al., 2017; Kaufman et al., 2008). The logical progression from observation to hypothesis is sound.

result: Route of administration determines the anatomical distribution and functional quality of antigen-specific CD8+ T cell responses. Intramuscular infection induces stronger systemic responses in blood and spleen, while intranasal infection generates superior responses in lungs, with differences in polyfunctional cytokine production.
evaluation: Claims C29-C33 are well-supported by tetramer staining (Figure 3B), intracellular cytokine staining (Figure 3C), and absolute cell counts (Figure 3—figure supplement 1) with appropriate statistical significance (p<0.01, p<0.05). The data comprehensively characterize route-dependent immune responses.

result: Intranasal infection results in retention of effector T cells in lungs through upregulation of tissue retention molecules (VLA-1, CXCR6, CD103, CD44) and increased frequencies of tissue-resident memory T cells (TRM).
evaluation: Claims C34-C38 are supported by flow cytometry data (Figure 3—figure supplement 2A-B) showing significant upregulation (p<0.0001) of retention markers and TRM frequencies. The interpretation is consistent with cited literature (Hogan et al., 2001; Jennrich et al., 2012; Ray et al., 2004).

result: Pre-existing immunity to influenza can be overcome by pseudotyping NY-ESO-1 S-FLU with mismatched HA. Mice pre-exposed to X31 virus show reduced CTL responses when reinfected with matched HA/NA but maintain responses with mismatched HA/NA (PR8).
evaluation: Claims C39-C43, C89 are supported by experimental data (Figure 4A-B, Figure 4—figure supplement 1) showing differential CTL responses based on HA matching with statistical significance (p<0.0001 for NP responses). This demonstrates a practical solution to pre-existing immunity, though NY-ESO-1 responses were reduced in both conditions in spleen (C43), suggesting incomplete rescue.

result: Intramuscular injection of NY-ESO-1 S-FLU virus reduces subcutaneous tumor growth with high infiltration of NY-ESO-1-specific CD8+ T cells into tumors, while intranasal infection fails to control subcutaneous tumors despite accumulation of T cells in lungs. Both routes reduce lung metastasis, but only intramuscular injection reduces splenic metastasis.
evaluation: Claims C44-C49 are well-supported by tumor growth curves (Figure 5A), flow cytometry (Figure 5B), and clonogenic assays (Figure 5C) with appropriate statistical analysis (p<0.05, p<0.01, p<0.001). The differential efficacy based on route and tumor location is clearly demonstrated.

result: NY-ESO-1 S-FLU virus demonstrates superior anti-tumor efficacy compared to other viral vaccine platforms (Hu Ad5 and Fowl Pox) in reducing tumor growth and metastasis, with comparable initial CTL responses but better outcomes after booster immunization.
evaluation: Claims C50-C54 are supported by comparative CTL data (Figure 5—figure supplement 1), tumor growth measurements (Figure 6A), and clonogenic assays (Figure 6B). The comparison with established platforms strengthens the significance, though mechanistic understanding of superior efficacy is limited.

result: Combination therapy of NY-ESO-1 S-FLU virus (intramuscular) with anti-PD1 antibody produces synergistic anti-tumor effects with the most pronounced tumor regression. Anti-PD1 does not increase T cell infiltration but upregulates CD103 expression on tumor-infiltrating CTLs and significantly reduces tumor metastasis.
evaluation: Claims C55-C61 are supported by tumor growth data (Figure 7B), flow cytometry showing PD1 expression and CD103 upregulation (Figure 7B), and clonogenic assays (Figure 7C) with statistical significance (p<0.05). The synergistic effect is clearly demonstrated, though the mechanism beyond CD103 upregulation requires further investigation.

result: The S-FLU virus system is similar to live-attenuated influenza vaccine (LAIV) in generating T cell mucosal immunity. Intranasal immunization induces robust lung CTL responses but modest systemic responses, with route of administration influencing the intensity of systemic responses.
evaluation: Claims C62-C65 are supported by citations (Korenkov et al., 2018; Powell et al., 2012; Nogales et al., 2016) and experimental data throughout the manuscript. The characterization appropriately contextualizes the system within existing vaccine platforms.

result: The observed route-dependent differences in systemic CTL responses are consistent with prior literature on influenza vaccine immunization routes, with intramuscular delivery generating stronger systemic responses.
evaluation: Claims C66-C68 are supported by appropriate citations (Trondsen et al., 2015; Bhide et al., 2019; Budimir et al., 2013) and align with the experimental observations. The comparison validates the findings within the broader literature.

result: The 4T1 mouse breast cancer model used resembles triple-negative breast tumors in humans, with tumor cells expressing lower levels of NY-ESO-1 potentially comparable to physiological expression in human cancer.
evaluation: Claim C69 is supported by citation (Luo et al., 2020), but C70 is speculative without direct measurement or comparison data. The relevance to human NY-ESO-1 expression levels is not validated experimentally.

result: Intranasal infection protects against lung metastasis but not subcutaneous tumors. GFP S-FLU alone provides partial protection, suggesting innate immune contributions via TLR7. Full metastasis reduction requires NY-ESO-1 expression, with regional protection attributed to lung-retained CTLs that fail to infiltrate distal tumors.
evaluation: Claims C71-C75 are supported by experimental data (Figures 2, 3) and appropriate speculation with citation (Chi et al., 2017). The mechanistic interpretation (C75) is reasonable inference from the T cell distribution data, though direct causation is not proven.

result: Tissue retention of T cells in lungs following intranasal infection may prevent migration to distal tumor sites, consistent with prior observations of T cell shunting during respiratory infections. Upregulation of retention molecules (VLA-1, CXCR6, CD103, CD44) likely contributes to this phenomenon.
evaluation: Claims C76-C77 are supported by citation (Newman et al., 2020) and tissue retention marker data (Figure 3—figure supplement 2A). The mechanistic interpretation is reasonable inference, though direct demonstration of impaired migration would strengthen the conclusion.

result: Intramuscular injection reduces primary tumor burden and metastasis to lungs and spleen, with high tumor infiltration of antigen-specific CD8+ T cells. Decreased metastasis is likely due to primary tumor regression rather than direct effects at metastatic sites.
evaluation: Claims C78-C80 are supported by experimental data (Figure 5C) and flow cytometry showing T cell distribution. The inference about mechanism (C80) is reasonable given the T cell distribution pattern, though alternative explanations are not fully excluded.

result: S-FLU virus induces comparable initial CTL responses to recombinant adenovirus but superior tumor regression after booster immunization. The weaker adenovirus efficacy may be due to anti-vector neutralizing antibodies from primary infection.
evaluation: Claims C81-C82 are supported by experimental data (Figure 5—figure supplement 1, Figure 6) and citation (Soboleski et al., 2011). Claim C83 is reasonable speculation supported by citation (Sumida et al., 2004), though direct measurement of neutralizing antibodies would strengthen the conclusion.

result: Recent evidence shows limitations of adenoviral vaccine boosting, with cellular responses not enhanced by booster immunization. Strategies like using different vectors or extending intervals have been suggested to improve efficacy.
evaluation: Claims C84-C85 are supported by appropriate citations (Folegatti et al., 2020; Sayedahmed et al., 2018). This contextualizes the superior boosting efficacy of S-FLU within current challenges in viral vector vaccines.

result: Pre-existing influenza immunity is a general concern for influenza-based vaccines, as most humans have reactive antibodies from natural infection or vaccination, with individual variation in breadth of cross-reactive antibodies.
evaluation: Claims C86-C88 represent established knowledge about influenza immunity in human populations. These are appropriately cited as general concerns that motivate the pseudotyping strategy.

result: PD-1 signaling mediates T cell suppression in tumors, and checkpoint inhibitors have achieved successful tumor reduction. Recent work shows enhanced anti-tumor effects when combining adenovirus-based vaccines with checkpoint inhibitors.
evaluation: Claims C90-C92 are supported by multiple appropriate citations (Zhang et al., 2009; Sato et al., 2005; Lin et al., 2015; Andrews et al., 2019; Errico, 2015; Tumeh et al., 2014; Philippou et al., 2020; McAuliffe et al., 2021). This provides strong rationale for the combination therapy approach.

result: Anti-PD1 antibody shows modest tumor reduction alone but displays synergistic effects when combined with intramuscular NY-ESO-1 S-FLU virus, with drastic reduction in tumor size. Limited dosing (3 administrations) was used due to hypersensitivity concerns in the 4T1 model.
evaluation: Claims C93-C94 are supported by experimental data (Figure 7). Claim C95 is appropriately justified by citation (Mall et al., 2016), though this limitation may have prevented observation of maximal therapeutic benefit.

result: Combination therapy upregulates CD103 expression on cytotoxic T cells, which correlates with tumor reduction. CD103 improves TCR antigen sensitivity and enables faster cancer recognition and anti-tumor cytotoxicity.
evaluation: Claim C96 is supported by experimental data (Figure 7B) showing correlation. Claim C97 is supported by citations (Qu et al., 2020; Abd Hamid et al., 2020) explaining the functional significance. However, the causal relationship between CD103 upregulation and tumor reduction is not directly demonstrated.

result: Virus-based tumor vaccines offer advantages over other delivery systems by generating concerted innate and adaptive responses. Prior approaches like DC vaccines had limited success due to tumor-suppressive environments, and checkpoint inhibitors leave many patients unaffected. Viruses are naturally immunogenic and more effective than soluble antigens, with influenza virus being a strong candidate for antigen delivery.
evaluation: Claims C98-C109 represent established knowledge and rationale supported by appropriate citations (Palucka and Banchereau, 2012; Shekarian et al., 2017; Kantor et al., 1992; Kass et al., 1999). This provides comprehensive background justifying the approach.
